What Went Wrong at Fortis Games?
By Miikka Ahonen •   November 22, 2026
Source: Fortis Games
On November 10,
Fortis Games shut down
after its owner, Las Vegas Sands, ended its funding, according to employees. More than 400 people lost their jobs. Six days earlier, Fortis had announced the closure of Twilight Towers, its first soft-launch title, because the game wasn’t retaining enough players.
Startups fail all the time, but Fortis was not just any startup. Wholly owned by Sands, it debuted in March 2022 with more than 150 employees, assembled by acquiring three studios, and nearly tripled in size from there. Yet it never brought a game to global launch.
That makes the closure worth examining beyond the layoffs. Fortis had money, talent, and an ambitious plan. What it couldn’t establish was a successful product. The changing games market and Sands’ shifting priorities help explain the timing of the shutdown, but the more basic question is whether Fortis’ strategy gave it a good chance of finding a hit in the first place.
The Promise of Patient Capital
In 2021, Las Vegas Sands (NYSE: LVS) was in a peculiar place. The pandemic had gutted its casino business, yet the company was about to come into a fortune, as it had agreed to sell its Las Vegas properties, including the Venetian, the Palazzo, and the Sands Expo convention center, for $6.25B. Alongside large resort projects in Asia, Sands began looking for digital businesses to put that money into.
Fortis was one of those bets. Patrick Dumont, then Sands’ president and COO (and married into the Adelson family that controls it),
promised to invest
“at scale for the long-term.” Fortis president (later CEO) Steven Chiang, in turn, said Fortis would create deeply social games that span different platforms and genres, but steer clear of casino games.
Fortis leadership had substantial industry experience. Chiang had run worldwide studios at WB Games, co-founded EA Tiburon, and served as president of studios at Zynga, while COO Shawn Foust was a former WB Games executive. Fortis acquired three studios to kickstart its operations: Doppio in Portugal, Oktagon in Brazil, and Metagame in Romania.
Rather than leaving them as independent teams, Fortis folded the studios into one distributed organization spanning North America, Europe, and Latin America. By August 2023, it had just over 300 employees, with roughly half a dozen game teams alongside central publishing, analytics, user acquisition, and community functions. By 2025, it was also talking about third-party publishing and further acquisitions.
Fortis set out from the start to build a company capable of making and running multiple games. In its pitch to recruits, it emphasized turning design innovation into a competitive advantage. In Fortis’ own language, its games would build “digital societies” and relationships that lasted for years.
There was something refreshing about the ambition. Mobile games typically stick to proven formulas, and for good reason. Free-to-play design templates are the result of years of survival-of-the-fittest evolution, and creating something genuinely new is a risky way to pursue a hit. Sands’ patient capital gave Fortis an unusual opportunity to try. But Fortis wasn’t just betting on design innovation. It was also building a large organization long before it was clear whether its games would work.
What Fortis Actually Built
Twilight Towers, a free-to-play game combining merge mechanics with tower defense, was the title that got the furthest. It was soft-launched in the Philippines and Mexico in September 2025, three and a half years after Fortis’ public debut. Over the following year, Fortis iterated on the game, reworking and adding features. On November 4,
Fortis pulled the game from the stores
. Its retention had not been strong enough to justify ongoing development.
Twilight Towers | Source: APKPure
Fortis’ other in-development titles included Bloom & Breakfast, a cozy merge game about running a bed and breakfast, which was soft-launched in the UK, the Philippines, and Canada, according to Sensor Tower. Another title, Mergemon Wilds, a creature-collection and merging game, was also in early soft launch. A fourth title,
Havoc Crew, a cooperative multiplayer dungeon crawler
, never reached soft launch.
Set against Fortis’ launch pitch, the portfolio is telling. The company promised deeply social games spanning platforms and genres. By the time it closed, three of its four known titles were mobile merge games, a typically single-player genre and one of the most crowded corners of casual mobile. The one game that fit the original pitch, the cooperative multiplayer Havoc Crew, never reached soft launch. There may have been others: after the closure, a Fortis lead
posted that her team had soft-launched two games
in four months, without naming them.
From the outside, it looks like a retreat. Patient capital was meant to free Fortis from proven formulas; the games we saw ended up in one of the most proven of all — and one where it had no particular edge.
Scale Before Product Validation
We have no visibility into the internal decision-making of Fortis, but the numbers are clear enough.
Fortis had 150 people at launch in 2022, just over 300 eighteen months later, and up to 440 at the time of closure. All without a single game reaching global launch. Each hire can make sense for a company that plans to run several live games. Each hire also adds to an ever-increasing overhead of fixed costs.
Sands has not disclosed how much it spent on Fortis, but with some back-of-the-napkin math, we can conservatively assume total investment in the low nine figures since 2022. Assuming an average workforce of 300 for four years at $120,000 a year per employee, we arrive at $144M in personnel costs alone.
